name: woid
workload: std::sort over vectors of ints (sizes 2^1 to 2^18) using a comparator wrapped in woid::Fun vs std::function vs function2 vs a plain lambda (bench/fun_bench.cpp, targets benchVectorStdLess and benchVectorBigLess)
claimed_speedup: README states woid::Fun 'ranks first in most cases' vs std::function/function2 across the FunBench suite; the cited plot (FunBench_benchVectorStdLess_speedup.svg) is titled 'Speedup vs. <std::function<bool(int, int)>>, times' with a y-axis scale of 1x-6x, but the exact per-vector-size ratio is only encoded in the SVG chart geometry, not as extractable text, so no single number is asserted here
compiler_and_flags: Clang 21.1.6 (also tested with GCC 15); CMakeLists.txt release flags include -O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-rtti (some configs add -fno-exceptions / -march=native)
tradeoffs: Requires C++23; woid::Fun/FunRef are type-erased wrappers with configurable SBO size/alignment (via woid::Any/TrivialAny storages) and, unlike std::function, they respect const/noexcept on the call signature; no separate move-only wrapper type is needed since copyability follows the chosen Storage instead. Benchmark also compares woid::Any vs std::any and woid::InterfaceBuilder vs virtual functions/boost::te/microsoft::proxy, so std::function is only one of several targets.
caveats: Single-author, single-machine benchmark (i9-10850K, Clang 21.1.6); only 7 GitHub stars and very new (first commits ~Jan 2026); the specific numeric speedup for the std::function comparator benchmark is only visible in an SVG plot image whose data is vector paths, not machine-readable text, so it could not be transcribed exactly here.
found_via: Hacker News — HN Algolia search "std::function faster" surfaced Show HN thread for akopich/woid ("Show HN: Woid – 3x Faster Runtime Polymorphism. C++23")

name: sy_callback.hpp
workload: 10 million repetitions each of: callback invocation (member/global/lambda), construction+destruction, and copy/move/assign, for sy_callback::callback<Signature> vs std::function; also a compile-time/binary-size test instantiating 1000 callbacks
claimed_speedup: README (README.ENG.md) tables: call time for lambda-without-capture ~0.041s (sy_callback) vs ~0.073s (std::function) (~1.8x faster, derived from page data); init+destroy for lambda-without-capture ~0.08s vs ~0.51s (~6.4x faster, derived from page data), and for large 1024-byte capture ~0.1s vs ~1.5s (~15x faster, derived from page data); move ~0.027s vs ~0.37s (~14x faster, derived from page data); assign ~0.26s vs ~1.9s (~7.3x faster, derived from page data)
hardware: Apple M1 (MacOS), exact chip variant unstated
tradeoffs: No small-buffer optimization — every callable except a non-capturing lambda is heap-allocated behind a raw pointer; not safe to move/destroy concurrently across threads (only copy is thread-safe); C++11-only API; docs are bilingual Vietnamese/English machine-translated text mixed into the README.
caveats: Numbers are first-party and only in the README — the repo contains no bench/ directory or benchmark source file (only a single test.cpp), so the runs cited are not independently reproducible from published code, even though compiler and hardware are named. Repo has 0 stars, single contributor, last pushed 2025-09-18 (~1 year before this search).
found_via: Hacker News — HN Algolia search "Show HN callback C++" surfaced Show HN thread "sy_callback.hpp – High-performance, header-only C++11 callback library"
